extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor economists, policymakers, regulated stakeholders, and public commenters on the DOL overtime rule
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and criteria for estimating the number and characteristics of workers affected by changes to the FLSA executive/administrative/professional (EAP) salary and HCE thresholds, and for estimating regulatory costs and transfers to employers and employees. Covers data choices, exclusions, probability models for duties, threshold-setting rules, and cost-estimation components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine FLSA coverage population
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify workers covered by the FLSA and subject to the Department's part 541 regulations (e.g., of 167.3 million wage and salary workers, estimate 143.7 million covered — 85.9 percent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for exclusions (Federal worker exceptions, firms with annual revenue < $500,000 engaged/not engaged in interstate commerce) and note data limitations that may prevent excluding some small populations. Use comparable approaches from prior rules (2004, 2016, 2019) where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude Federal employees exempted by statute or agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize exceptions for U.S. Postal Service employees, Tennessee Valley Authority employees, and Library of Congress employees when identifying covered Federal workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include covered Federal workers using occupation and/or industry codes and remove other Federal employees; follow prior rule practice for identifying these populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude workers unlikely to be affected (blue-collar, hourly, non-EAP exemptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: After limiting analysis to FLSA-covered workers subject to part 541, identify and exclude blue-collar workers, workers paid on an hourly basis, and workers exempt under other (non-EAP) exemptions because the final rule is unlikely to affect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methodologies from GAO 1999 white-collar exemptions report and prior DOL RIAs; supervisors in blue-collar industries may be classified as white-collar if duties are managerial/administrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and exclude agricultural and transportation worker subgroups when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude agricultural and transportation workers from further analysis where they qualify for the agricultural or specified transportation overtime pay exemptions, using occupation-industry combinations consistent with recent rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow precedent: 2004 excluded all agricultural industry workers; recent rules excluded only specific occupation-industry combos. Transportation workers defined by list of relevant FLSA exemptions (13(b)(1), 13(b)(2), 13(b)(3), 13(b)(6), 13(b)(10)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the population of salaried white-collar workers
rubrics_metrics.description: After exclusions, estimate the number of salaried white-collar workers for whom employers might claim either the standard EAP exemption or the HCE exemption (e.g., 53.5 million in this analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document all prior exclusions and reference Appendix A for detailed identification criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard EAP exemption tests (three-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be exempt under the standard EAP test, the employee generally must: (1) be paid a predetermined and fixed salary not subject to reduction because of variations in quality or quantity of work (salary basis test); (2) earn at least a designated salary amount (standard salary level test, currently $684/week previously); and (3) primarily perform exempt work as defined by the regulations (standard duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three prongs when estimating current exemption status; treat named occupations differently where earnings thresholds do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly Compensated Employee (HCE) test
rubrics_metrics.description: HCE test allows certain highly paid employees to qualify for exemption if they customarily and regularly perform one or more exempt job duties (HCE duties test) and meet an annual compensation threshold (current HCE annual compensation level and requirement that includes at least $684/week paid on a salary or fee basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for HCE by supplementing standard duties probability codes to reflect more lenient duties probabilities for high-earning workers; update compensation thresholds when set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary basis proxy in CPS: use nonhourly workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only nonhourly workers in the analysis based on CPS data and consider CPS 'nonhourly' compensation as an appropriate proxy for salaried workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge CPS nonhourly includes piece rate, day rate, bonuses, commissions; validate with PSID showing relatively few nonhourly paid by methods other than salaried; note lack of a statistically robust data source that more closely reflects regulatory salary definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for CPS earnings variable limitations (bonuses, commissions, overtime, tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize CPS includes nondiscretionary bonuses and commissions, includes overtime pay, and includes tips and discretionary commissions which do not all qualify under regulation; these measurement differences may over- or under-estimate counts meeting salary/HCE tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust estimation approach or note direction of possible bias; remember regulation allows nondiscretionary bonuses/commissions to satisfy up to 10% of standard salary level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topcoding and imputation for high earners in CPS
rubrics_metrics.description: CPS annual earnings variable is topcoded at $150,000 (reported as $2,884.61/week); impute earnings for topcoded workers to adequately estimate impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document imputation approach and its potential effects on HCE and salary estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate duties test passing probability using occupational probability codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because CPS MORG lacks duties info, use WHD/GAO 1998/1999 analysis assigning probability codes (four codes reflecting ranges) to occupational codes indicating likelihood a worker performs duties meeting EAP duties tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same methodology as prior rulemakings (2004, 2016, 2019); list all occupations and probability codes in Appendix A; acknowledge age of codes but justify continued use via O*NET checks and lack of better alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map older occupational probability codes to current occupational classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1999 GAO occupations map to 1990 Census codes; use occupational crosswalks to map to 2018 Census occupational codes used in CPS MORG 2021–2023 data. If a new occupation comprises more than one previous occupation, compute weighted average probability code rounded to nearest code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document mapping and weighting method; preserve probability code semantics when aggregating or splitting occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify probability codes for HCE duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement and modify the four probability codes to reflect probabilities of passing the more lenient HCE duties test based on analysis of the HCE provisions relative to the standard duties test (e.g., occupation with standard code 4 may get higher HCE probability if earnings exceed HCE level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how probabilities change with earnings; provide examples (e.g., first-line supervisors/managers of construction trades assigned code 4 with 0–10% for standard but 15% if earning at/above HCE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine occupation probability and earnings to estimate individual exemption probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the probability of qualifying for the standard exemption for each worker as a function of both earnings and the occupation's exempt probability category using a gamma distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naive random assignment ignoring earnings; use distributions that increase exemption probability with earnings to reflect real-world correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign exemption status by stochastic draw using individual probability
rubrics_metrics.description: For each worker, assign exempt/nonexempt status via a random draw from a binomial distribution with the worker's revised probability as the probability of success (e.g., if probability = 60%, expect 6 of 10 to be designated exempt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the randomization approach and seed/reporting to ensure reproducibility; refer to Appendix A for implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude named occupations from earnings-based impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude certain named occupations (physicians, lawyers, teachers, academic administrative personnel, outside sales workers) from consideration of the earnings thresholds because they are not required to pass the salary requirements (they still must pass duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific Census occupation and industry codes for named occupations; remove these workers when estimating number affected by salary/HCE changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'potentially affected' vs 'affected' worker populations
rubrics_metrics.description: After exclusions, label remaining EAP-exempt workers as 'potentially affected' (e.g., 29.7 million) and estimate the subset who will be actually affected in Year 1 by the salary/HCE increases (e.g., 4.3 million total; 4.0M affected by standard salary change; 292,900 by HCE change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish workers whose exemption status would 'turn on their job duties' from those whose earnings place them below thresholds irrespective of duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set standard salary level using percentile of earnings in lowest-wage Census region
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the standard salary level using the 35th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census region (currently the South), using 2023 CPS data in this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify selection of percentile and region; document data year and source; explain any semi-annual/periodic update mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set HCE compensation level using nationwide percentile
rubrics_metrics.description: Set HCE compensation level at the annualized weekly earnings of the 85th percentile of full-time salaried workers nationwide, using CPS data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document exact percentile and data source/year; explain connection between percentile choice and policy objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize overtime worker types for impact analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and separately analyze 'regular overtime workers' (typically worked >40 hours/week) and 'occasional overtime workers' (typically ≤40 hours/week but worked >40 hours in the survey week), because labor market responses may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate mean overtime hours and earnings by type; note that many affected workers do not usually work overtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate employer costs in three categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify three direct costs to employers: (1) regulatory familiarization costs; (2) adjustment costs; and (3) managerial costs (same categories as 2016 and 2019 rulemakings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide Year 1 and annualized multi-year estimates; discuss additional potential but unquantified costs (reduced profits, hiring changes) in narrative sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory familiarization cost estimation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate familiarization costs by determining (1) the number of affected establishments/entities; (2) a wage level for employees reviewing the rule; and (3) the time spent reviewing the rule. Assume decentralized familiarization at establishment level (8.15M establishments + 90,126 state/local governments = 8.24M entities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume 1 hour average per entity, use SOC 13-1141 compensation/job analysts with median wage $32.59/hour, benefits at 45% of base wage, overhead at 17% of base wage, resulting in $54.82/hour in 2023 dollars; multiply hourly rate × 1 hour × entities to get total familiarization cost. Conduct sensitivity analysis using number of firms instead of establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalize assumptions for time and reviewer type used in regulatory familiarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify using 1 hour average because EAP exemptions are long-standing and employers are familiar; use compensation/job analysis specialists as the reviewer occupation used in prior WHD/DOL rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address stakeholder comments that reviewing may take longer; separate additional compliance/implementation time into managerial and adjustment cost categories rather than familiarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment cost components for employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate costs to evaluate exemption status, update and adapt overtime policies, notify employees of policy changes, and adjust payroll systems; for each affected overtime-working employee employers will decide to increase salary, adjust hours, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify these costs using methodologies consistent with prior rulemakings and include both Year 1 and recurring costs; discuss assumptions on employer responses and likely variation by worker characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and respond to commenter criticisms of methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenters assert outdated or flawed probability codes or raise higher estimates, document their claims (e.g., Oxford Economics, AFPI) and provide justification for continuing to use existing methods (mapping, O*NET review, precedent) or explain why commenters' alternative approaches miscount workers by ignoring the duties test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterate methodological defenses in the record: updated mapping, similarity of duties test to former tests, use of O*NET to verify appropriateness, and explanation why earnings-only estimates overstate affected counts by ignoring duties test.
